taxonomy.subtopic: Intact Sertoli-cell anti-Müllerian hormone with absent androgen-receptor action

questions.stem_html: A 16-year-old adolescent with a female phenotype is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. Breast development is normal, pubic and axillary hair is sparse, and the vagina ends blindly. Imaging shows no uterus and identifies bilateral inguinal gonads. Karyotype is 46,XY. The accompanying embryology map shows regression of one duct system despite failure of external virilization. Which fetal signal remained functionally intact?

options.text_html: Anti-Müllerian hormone secretion by Sertoli cells
Dihydrotestosterone binding to androgen receptors in genital skin

questions.explanation_html: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, testes form and Sertoli cells secrete anti-Müllerian hormone, so the Müllerian ducts regress and the uterus, cervix and upper vagina are absent. Leydig cells produce testosterone, but defective androgen receptors prevent testosterone-dependent Wolffian differentiation and dihydrotestosterone-dependent external virilization. Aromatization of androgens supports breast development at puberty.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Dihydrotestosterone action is ineffective because the androgen receptor is defective; this explains female external genitalia and sparse body hair.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Wolffian duct differentiation requires testosterone acting through a functional androgen receptor and is therefore absent or rudimentary.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Fetal ovaries are not present in a 46,XY individual with testes.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Ovarian follicle differentiation is not the mechanism; SRY-driven testicular development has occurred.

questions.educational_objective: Complete androgen insensitivity preserves Sertoli-cell anti-Müllerian hormone and Müllerian regression while blocking androgen-dependent Wolffian development and external virilization.

media.alt_text: Original fetal sex-differentiation map showing testes, intact anti-Müllerian hormone, Müllerian regression and failed androgen-receptor signaling.
